course_title: Practical Exercise on European and Global Legal History
title: Questions and sources, exercise class V — natural law, sovereignty, constitutionalism

slides.title: The beginnings of natural-law thinking in antiquity
slides.text: A supplementary question to Digest I.1.9. THE ROOTS: (1) GREEK TRAGEDY AND PHILOSOPHY — SOPHOCLES' ANTIGONE is the oldest famous formulation: against Creon's prohibition of burying her brother, Antigone invokes the 'UNWRITTEN AND UNSHAKEABLE LAWS OF THE GODS', which are not of today or yesterday and of whose origin no one knows. It is the germ of the idea that above a positive command stands a higher norm. (2) THE SOPHISTS set PHYSIS (nature) against NOMOS (enactment), and some of them (Antiphon, Callicles) concluded that law is merely a human convention, often against nature — which is the critical, not the constructive version. (3) ARISTOTLE distinguished NATURAL justice (physikon dikaion), which holds the same everywhere, from LEGAL justice (nomikon), which is a matter of enactment. (4) STOICISM is the most important for legal history: it teaches that the world is governed by REASON (LOGOS), that all human beings share in it, and therefore that they are by nature EQUAL and form one world community (KOSMOPOLIS). From this comes the universalism that in Europe outlives everything else. (5) CICERO translates the idea into Latin and into juristic language in a passage worth knowing: true law is RIGHT REASON IN AGREEMENT WITH NATURE, it applies among all peoples and at all times, it cannot be repealed by senate or people, and whoever disobeys it flees from himself. (6) THE ROMAN JURISTS then draw natural law into doctrine — in Ulpian as what nature has taught all animals, in Gaius merging with the ius gentium. HOW THIS DIFFERS FROM TODAY'S UNDERSTANDING OF THE LAW OF NATIONS: ancient natural law is (a) MORAL-COSMIC, not interstate; (b) ADDRESSED NOT TO STATES but to human beings; (c) NOT ENFORCEABLE BY ANY INSTITUTION; (d) and its content is ascertained by RATIONAL REFLECTION, not by agreement. Today's international law, by contrast, is POSITIVE, INTERSTATE AND BASED ON CONSENT — and the natural-law argument survives in it only in the form of ius cogens and human rights.

terms.def: Nature against enactment — the sophistic distinction out of which the tension between natural and positive law grows.

cards.q: Where does natural-law thinking have its roots in antiquity?
cards.a: SOPHOCLES' ANTIGONE ('the unwritten and unshakeable laws of the gods'); THE SOPHISTS with the distinction PHYSIS × NOMOS; ARISTOTLE with NATURAL and LEGAL justice; STOICISM with the rule of REASON (LOGOS), the natural equality of human beings and KOSMOPOLIS; CICERO ('true law is RIGHT REASON IN AGREEMENT WITH NATURE', it cannot be repealed by senate or people); and THE ROMAN JURISTS, who drew it into doctrine.

cards.q: How does ancient natural law differ from today's law of nations?
cards.a: The ancient is MORAL-COSMIC, not interstate; it is addressed to HUMAN BEINGS, not states; it is NOT ENFORCEABLE by any institution; and its content is ascertained by RATIONAL REFLECTION, not by agreement. Today's international law is POSITIVE, INTERSTATE AND BASED ON CONSENT — the natural-law argument survives in it only in ius cogens and human rights.

slides.title: The transformation of public law between 1648 and the 19th century
slides.text: The question calls for EVENTS, THINKERS AND THEORIES, that is, three axes at once. THE STARTING POINT (1648): the PEACE OF WESTPHALIA establishes the SOVEREIGNTY OF THE TERRITORIAL LORDS, the principle CUIUS REGIO, EIUS RELIGIO is softened into religious coexistence, and the international order is founded on the EQUALITY OF SOVEREIGNS without a superior authority. Within the states ABSOLUTISM takes over. THE EVENTS THAT LEAD ON: the ENGLISH CIVIL WAR AND THE GLORIOUS REVOLUTION (1688–89) with the BILL OF RIGHTS; the AMERICAN REVOLUTION (the Declaration of Independence 1776, the Constitution 1787, the Bill of Rights 1791); the FRENCH REVOLUTION (1789, the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen, the constitutions of 1791 and 1793); the NAPOLEONIC WARS and with them the export of revolutionary institutions and of the Code civil; the CONGRESS OF VIENNA (1814–15) and the Restoration; and 1848 as a wave of constitutional revolutions. THE THINKERS AND THEIR THEORIES: HOBBES (Leviathan 1651) — the state of nature as a war of all against all, a SOCIAL CONTRACT by which power is irrevocably transferred to the sovereign; LOCKE (Two Treatises 1689) — natural rights to LIFE, LIBERTY AND PROPERTY, government as a TRUST and, where it is broken, a RIGHT OF RESISTANCE; MONTESQUIEU (The Spirit of the Laws 1748) — the SEPARATION OF POWERS and the idea that power must check power; ROUSSEAU (The Social Contract 1762) — the SOVEREIGNTY OF THE PEOPLE and the GENERAL WILL; PUFENDORF, THOMASIUS AND WOLFF — rational natural law, which gives the legislator the ambition to codify; BECCARIA (1764) — the humanization of criminal law; KANT — the Rechtsstaat and autonomy; SIEYÈS — the CONSTITUENT POWER (pouvoir constituant) and the concept of the nation. THE RESULTING TRANSFORMATION IN THREE POINTS: (1) FROM THE SOVEREIGNTY OF THE RULER TO THE SOVEREIGNTY OF THE PEOPLE OR THE NATION; (2) FROM SUBJECT TO CITIZEN WITH RIGHTS, that is, the emergence of a catalogue of fundamental rights; (3) FROM UNLIMITED POWER TO POWER DIVIDED AND BOUND BY A CONSTITUTION. This is called, in sum, CONSTITUTIONALISM.

cards.q: Name the thinkers and their theories that transformed public law between 1648 and the 19th century.
cards.a: HOBBES (Leviathan 1651) — the war of all against all and the irrevocable transfer of power to the sovereign. LOCKE (1689) — rights to LIFE, LIBERTY AND PROPERTY, government as a TRUST and a RIGHT OF RESISTANCE. MONTESQUIEU (1748) — the SEPARATION OF POWERS. ROUSSEAU (1762) — the SOVEREIGNTY OF THE PEOPLE and the GENERAL WILL. PUFENDORF, THOMASIUS, WOLFF — rational natural law. BECCARIA (1764) — the humanization of criminal law. KANT — the Rechtsstaat. SIEYÈS — the CONSTITUENT POWER and the nation.

cards.q: Sum up the transformation of public law 1648–19th century in three points.
cards.a: 1) FROM THE SOVEREIGNTY OF THE RULER TO THE SOVEREIGNTY OF THE PEOPLE OR THE NATION. 2) FROM SUBJECT TO CITIZEN WITH RIGHTS, that is, the emergence of a catalogue of fundamental rights. 3) FROM UNLIMITED POWER TO POWER DIVIDED AND BOUND BY A CONSTITUTION. In sum, CONSTITUTIONALISM.

slides.title: Source: the frontispiece of Hobbes's Leviathan (1651)
slides.text: WHAT CAN BE SEEN IN THE PICTURE: above a landscape with a town, fields and hills rises the ENORMOUS FIGURE OF A CROWNED RULER from the waist up. His BODY IS COMPOSED OF HUNDREDS OF SMALL HUMAN FIGURES, turned inwards, towards the head — we see their backs, not their faces. IN HIS RIGHT HAND HE HOLDS A SWORD, in his LEFT A BISHOP'S CROSIER. Below the picture are two columns of emblems: on the left the temporal (a fortress, a crown, a cannon, weapons, a battle), on the right the ecclesiastical (a church, a mitre, the thunderbolts of excommunication, the distinctions of concepts, a council). Above is a quotation from the Book of Job: 'NON EST POTESTAS SUPER TERRAM QUAE COMPARETUR EI' — there is no power on earth to compare with him. WHAT THIS TELLS US ABOUT THE SOVEREIGN'S POSITION: (1) he is ONE AND INDIVISIBLE; (2) HE IS LITERALLY COMPOSED OF HIS SUBJECTS — his power is theirs merged together, so that he is not above them from outside but IS them; (3) he holds BOTH SWORD AND CROSIER, that is, TEMPORAL AND SPIRITUAL POWER IN ONE HAND, which is a direct attack on the doctrine of the two swords and on the church's claim; (4) he stands ABOVE THE TOWN, which lies beneath him peaceful and empty — the peace is his work. ON THE TASK OF THE STATE: to secure PEACE AND SAFETY, because that is the one thing people lack in the state of nature. HOW THE PICTURE ILLUSTRATES THE THEORY: Hobbes teaches that in the STATE OF NATURE there is BELLUM OMNIUM CONTRA OMNES, the war of all against all, and life is 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish and short'. Out of the FEAR OF VIOLENT DEATH people conclude a SOCIAL CONTRACT: not with the sovereign but WITH ONE ANOTHER, and by it they give up the right to all things in favour of one bearer. That is why the sovereign in the picture is COMPOSED OF THEM — he is their AUTHORIZED PERSON, not an alien power. And that is also why HE IS NOT A PARTY TO THE CONTRACT, cannot break it, and the subjects have no right of resistance, with one exception: if he threatens their bare life, for the protection of which the contract was made.

terms.def: The war of all against all — Hobbes's state of nature, from which one emerges by the social contract.

cards.q: Describe the frontispiece of Hobbes's Leviathan and what follows from it about the sovereign.
cards.a: An enormous CROWNED RULER above a landscape, whose BODY IS COMPOSED OF HUNDREDS OF HUMAN FIGURES turned towards the head; in his right hand a SWORD, in his left a BISHOP'S CROSIER; above, the quotation from Job 'THERE IS NO POWER ON EARTH TO COMPARE WITH HIM'. It follows that the sovereign is ONE AND INDIVISIBLE, IS COMPOSED OF HIS SUBJECTS (their power merged, not above them from outside) and holds TEMPORAL AND SPIRITUAL POWER in one hand.
cards.topic: The Westphalian Order and Early Constitutionalism

cards.q: How does the picture illustrate Hobbes's theory?
cards.a: In the STATE OF NATURE there is BELLUM OMNIUM CONTRA OMNES and life is 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish and short'. Out of the FEAR OF VIOLENT DEATH people conclude a contract NOT WITH THE SOVEREIGN BUT WITH ONE ANOTHER — which is why the sovereign in the picture is COMPOSED of them, he is their AUTHORIZED PERSON. That is also why HE IS NOT A PARTY TO THE CONTRACT and cannot break it; resistance is possible only where bare life is threatened.
cards.topic: The Westphalian Order and Early Constitutionalism

slides.title: Source: Vitoria, De Indiis (1538)
slides.text: THE SOURCE: 'The Spaniards may lawfully trade among the barbarians, so long as they do no harm to their country. That is to say, they may import the goods which the barbarians lack and export gold, silver or other things of which they have an abundance; and their princes may not prevent their subjects from trading with the Spaniards, nor may the princes of Spain prohibit trade with the barbarians… THE LAW OF NATIONS (IUS GENTIUM) is evidently such that travellers may carry on trade so long as they do no harm to the citizens… Any human enactment (LEX) that prohibited such trade would undoubtedly be unreasonable.' THE AUTHOR AND THE CONTEXT: FRANCISCO DE VITORIA (c. 1483–1546), a Dominican and professor at SALAMANCA, founder of the SCHOOL OF SALAMANCA or SECOND SCHOLASTICISM. The lecture De Indiis (1538/39) responds to the CONQUEST OF AMERICA and to the dispute whether and by what it can be justified. The current of thought: THOMIST NATURAL LAW, that is, Aquinas's doctrine elaborated for the new overseas questions. THE LEGAL ARGUMENT IN THE EXTRACT: Vitoria first REJECTED the traditional titles of conquest (papal grant, the emperor's universal power, the sin and unbelief of the Indians, their alleged incapacity) and acknowledged that THE INDIANS ARE THE TRUE OWNERS OF THEIR LANDS AND HAVE THEIR OWN LEGITIMATE GOVERNMENT. At the same time, however, he formulated LEGITIMATE TITLES, the first and most important of which is the RIGHT OF COMMUNICATION AND TRADE (IUS COMMUNICATIONIS ET COMMERCII): people have by nature the right to travel, to stay and to trade, so long as they do no harm. And here is the trap the question is after: THE DENIAL OF THAT RIGHT IS A WRONG, AND A WRONG JUSTIFIES DEFENCE, THAT IS, WAR — so that a noble principle turns into a JUSTIFICATION OF CONQUEST. THE RELATION OF LEX AND IUS GENTIUM: human enactment (lex) is SUBORDINATE to the law of nations, which flows from natural reason; a statute contrary to the ius gentium is 'unreasonable', that is, invalid. THE INFLUENCE ON GROTIUS AND THE DIFFERENCE: Grotius (De iure praedae, Mare liberum 1609, De iure belli ac pacis 1625) TOOK OVER Vitoria's argument and used it in favour of DUTCH TRADE against the Portuguese monopoly — the freedom of the seas is the same idea of the ius communicationis. HE DIFFERS, however, in that (1) Grotius SECULARIZES natural law (it would hold 'even if there were no God', etiamsi daremus non esse Deum), whereas Vitoria remains a theologian; (2) alongside natural law Grotius sets the IUS VOLUNTARIUM, the law arising from the consent of states, and thereby founds positive international law; (3) Vitoria thinks in terms of a single human community (totus orbis), Grotius already in terms of a SYSTEM OF SOVEREIGN STATES.

terms.def: The right of communication, travel and trade; in Vitoria a legitimate title whose denial justifies war.

cards.q: Who was Vitoria, and what did he reject and what acknowledge in De Indiis?
cards.a: FRANCISCO DE VITORIA (c. 1483–1546), a Dominican and professor at SALAMANCA, founder of the SCHOOL OF SALAMANCA (second scholasticism), Thomist natural law. He REJECTED the traditional titles of conquest (papal grant, the emperor's universal power, the sin and unbelief of the Indians) and acknowledged that THE INDIANS ARE THE TRUE OWNERS OF THEIR LANDS and have a legitimate government.
cards.topic: The Westphalian Order and Early Constitutionalism

cards.q: How does Vitoria's ius communicationis turn into a justification of conquest?
cards.a: People have by nature the RIGHT TO TRAVEL, TO STAY AND TO TRADE so long as they do no harm. BUT THE DENIAL OF THAT RIGHT IS A WRONG, AND A WRONG JUSTIFIES DEFENCE, THAT IS, WAR — so that a noble principle becomes a legitimate title of conquest.
cards.topic: The Westphalian Order and Early Constitutionalism

cards.q: How did Grotius use Vitoria's argument and how does he differ from him?
cards.a: He TOOK IT OVER in favour of DUTCH TRADE against the Portuguese monopoly (Mare liberum 1609) — the freedom of the seas is the same idea. HE DIFFERS: 1) Grotius SECULARIZES natural law ('etiamsi daremus non esse Deum'), Vitoria remains a theologian. 2) Grotius sets beside it the IUS VOLUNTARIUM, the law from the consent of states, founding positive international law. 3) Vitoria thinks in terms of a single humanity (totus orbis), Grotius already in a SYSTEM OF SOVEREIGN STATES.
cards.topic: The Westphalian Order and Early Constitutionalism

slides.title: Source: Vattel and the legal titles of colonization
slides.text: THE SOURCE: 'The whole earth is designed to feed its inhabitants; but it would be incapable of doing so if it were uncultivated. Every nation is therefore bound by the law of nature to cultivate the land that has fallen to its share, and it has no right to enlarge its boundaries or have recourse to the assistance of other nations but in proportion as the land in its possession is incapable of furnishing it with necessaries. Those nations which, like the ancient Germans and some modern Tartars, inhabit fertile countries but disdain to cultivate the earth and choose rather to live by plunder, are wanting to themselves, are injurious to all their neighbours AND DESERVE TO BE EXTERMINATED AS SAVAGE AND PERNICIOUS BEASTS.' (Le droit des gens, 1758, II.VII.§97.) VATTEL'S ROLE IN COLONIZATION: EMER DE VATTEL (1714–1767), a Swiss in the service of the Elector of Saxony, wrote the most influential handbook of international law of the 18th and 19th centuries — it was read in ministries and courts, and in the USA directly as an authority. His twofold contribution to colonization: (1) THE AGRICULTURAL ARGUMENT you see in the extract — THE DUTY TO CULTIVATE THE LAND makes uncultivated land land to which the claim is weaker, so that hunter-gatherer and nomadic peoples in effect lose title to territory; (2) he thereby links up with LOCKE'S LABOUR ARGUMENT (whoever mixes his labour with the soil acquires it) and with the concept of TERRA NULLIUS, land belonging to no one, which may be taken by OCCUPATION. THE LEGAL TITLES OF COLONIZATION the question calls for, then, in survey: (a) the PAPAL BULLS and the Treaty of TORDESILLAS (1494), dividing the world between Spain and Portugal; (b) DISCOVERY and SYMBOLIC TAKING; (c) THE OCCUPATION OF TERRA NULLIUS, where it is claimed that a territory belongs to no one or that its inhabitants have no recognizable government; (d) CONQUEST in a just war, for which Vitoria's titles serve; (e) TREATIES WITH INDIGENOUS RULERS, whose validity is often doubtful (language, coercion, a different conception of land); (f) CESSION between colonial powers; (g) in the 19th century PROTECTORATES and the FINAL ACT OF THE BERLIN CONFERENCE (1885) with its requirement of EFFECTIVE OCCUPATION; (h) and the CIVILIZING MISSION as an ideological justification, which then settles legally into the MANDATE SYSTEM (Art. 22 of the Covenant of the League of Nations, 1919). A CRITICISM MUST BE ADDED TO THE SOURCE: the sentence about extermination as savage beasts shows how natural-law argument about duties to oneself served to exclude whole peoples from the protection of law.

terms.def: Land belonging to no one — territory regarded as unoccupied or without a recognizable government, and therefore acquirable by occupation.

cards.q: What role did Vattel play in colonization?
cards.a: EMER DE VATTEL (1714–1767) wrote the most influential handbook of international law of the 18th–19th centuries. A twofold contribution: 1) THE AGRICULTURAL ARGUMENT — THE DUTY TO CULTIVATE THE LAND makes uncultivated land land to which the claim is weaker, so that HUNTER-GATHERER AND NOMADIC PEOPLES IN EFFECT LOSE TITLE TO TERRITORY. 2) He links up with LOCKE'S LABOUR ARGUMENT and the concept of TERRA NULLIUS.

cards.q: Which legal titles served for colonization?
cards.a: The PAPAL BULLS and TORDESILLAS (1494); DISCOVERY and symbolic taking; THE OCCUPATION OF TERRA NULLIUS; CONQUEST in a just war; TREATIES WITH INDIGENOUS RULERS (often doubtful); CESSION between powers; in the 19th century PROTECTORATES and the BERLIN CONFERENCE (1885) with its requirement of EFFECTIVE OCCUPATION; and the CIVILIZING MISSION, which settles legally into the MANDATE SYSTEM (Art. 22 of the Covenant, 1919).

slides.title: Source: Art. 16 of the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen (1789)
slides.text: THE SOURCE: 'A society in which the guarantee of rights is not secured, nor the separation of powers determined, has no constitution.' (Déclaration des droits de l'homme et du citoyen, Art. 16.) ON THE DOCUMENT IN GENERAL: it was adopted by the CONSTITUENT NATIONAL ASSEMBLY ON 26 AUGUST 1789, a few weeks after the fall of the Bastille, as a PREAMBLE TO A FUTURE CONSTITUTION (which it became in the constitution of 1791). It has 17 articles and its character is twofold: it is at once a PHILOSOPHICAL PROCLAMATION OF NATURAL RIGHTS ('men are born and remain free and equal in rights', Art. 1) AND A LEGAL ACT. The rights are conceived as NATURAL, INALIENABLE AND SACRED — the state does not give them, it only recognizes and protects them; and their only limit is the like freedom of others (Art. 4). The models were the American declarations (the Virginia Bill of Rights 1776) and the British tradition; the principal author of the draft was LAFAYETTE, in collaboration with JEFFERSON. The Declaration is still in force in France today as part of the CONSTITUTIONAL BLOC. WHERE IN ART. 16 WE HEAR LOCKE AND MONTESQUIEU: LOCKE is in the first half of the sentence — in the idea that the purpose of government is the SECURING OF NATURAL RIGHTS (life, liberty, property), that power is a TRUST for that purpose, and that a government which does not protect rights loses its legitimacy. MONTESQUIEU is in the second half — the SEPARATION OF POWERS into legislative, executive and judicial, because 'so that power may not be abused, POWER MUST CHECK POWER' (The Spirit of the Laws, 1748). AND THE ESSENTIAL THING IS THE COMBINATION OF THE TWO: Article 16 does not make rights and the separation of powers two wishes but TWO CONDITIONS WITHOUT WHICH THERE IS NO CONSTITUTION AT ALL. Thereby the descriptive concept of a constitution (any arrangement whatever) becomes a NORMATIVE one — henceforth only an arrangement that satisfies both will be called a constitution.

cards.q: What is the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen and what is its character?
cards.a: It was adopted by the CONSTITUENT NATIONAL ASSEMBLY ON 26 AUGUST 1789 as a PREAMBLE to a future constitution; 17 articles. Its character is TWOFOLD: a philosophical proclamation of NATURAL RIGHTS ('men are born and remain free and equal in rights') and a LEGAL ACT. The rights are NATURAL, INALIENABLE AND SACRED — the state does not give them, it only recognizes them. In France it is still in force as part of the CONSTITUTIONAL BLOC.

cards.q: Where in Art. 16 is Locke to be heard and where Montesquieu?
cards.a: LOCKE in the first half — the purpose of government is the SECURING OF NATURAL RIGHTS, power is a TRUST, and a government that does not protect rights loses its legitimacy. MONTESQUIEU in the second — the SEPARATION OF POWERS, because 'so that power may not be abused, POWER MUST CHECK POWER'. The essential thing is their COMBINATION: they are not two wishes but TWO CONDITIONS WITHOUT WHICH THERE IS NO CONSTITUTION AT ALL.

slides.title: Constitutionalism: ideas, beginnings, diffusion
slides.text: THE PHILOSOPHICAL IDEAS THAT PREPARED IT: (1) RATIONAL NATURAL LAW — a human being has rights that are not the ruler's gift; (2) THE SOCIAL CONTRACT as the source of the legitimacy of power (Hobbes, Locke, Rousseau); (3) THE SEPARATION OF POWERS (Locke, Montesquieu); (4) THE SOVEREIGNTY OF THE PEOPLE AND THE CONSTITUENT POWER (Rousseau, Sieyès); (5) THE IDEA OF A WRITTEN BASIC LAW as a higher norm, taken in part from the English charters and from colonial charters of foundation. WHERE AND WHEN FIRST: in its modern form in NORTH AMERICA — the constitutions of the individual states from 1776, the VIRGINIA BILL OF RIGHTS (1776), and the FEDERAL CONSTITUTION OF THE USA (1787, in force 1789) with the BILL OF RIGHTS (1791). THE POLITICAL CONTEXT is the key: it was necessary TO REGULATE THE RELATIONS OF THE FORMER COLONIES AFTER THE BREAK WITH THE CROWN, that is, to build a state on a green field, without a monarch and without a historical constitution — so the order had to be WRITTEN DOWN, and hence the constitution arises as A SINGLE DOCUMENT ISSUED BY THE PEOPLE. In Europe FRANCE follows (1791) in the context of the revolution. THE STEPS OF ITS DIFFUSION ACROSS EUROPE: (1) THE REVOLUTIONARY AND NAPOLEONIC PERIOD 1791–1815 — constitutions exported by French expansion, often short-lived; (2) 1812 THE SPANISH CONSTITUTION OF CÁDIZ, a model for southern Europe and Latin America; (3) AFTER THE CONGRESS OF VIENNA a wave of OCTROYED constitutions, that is, granted by the ruler from above — the FRENCH CHARTE (1814), the south German states (Bavaria and Baden 1818, Württemberg 1819) — and with them arises the type of MONARCHICAL CONSTITUTIONALISM, in which the ruler remains the source of power and the constitution merely limits it; (4) THE BELGIAN CONSTITUTION OF 1831 as the most liberal model of the century; (5) THE REVOLUTIONS OF 1848 — a wave of constitutions across Europe, including Austria (the Pillersdorf) and the Frankfurt Paulskirche; (6) THE SECOND HALF OF THE 19TH CENTURY — constitutions stabilize (Austria 1867, the German Empire 1871) and are supplemented by judicial guarantees; (7) AFTER 1918 — republican constitutions with constitutional jurisdiction (Austria 1920).

terms.def: A constitution granted by the ruler from above, not adopted by the constituent power of the people.

cards.q: Where and when did modern constitutionalism arise, and what was the political context?
cards.a: In NORTH AMERICA: the constitutions of the individual states from 1776, the VIRGINIA BILL OF RIGHTS (1776), the FEDERAL CONSTITUTION OF THE USA (1787, in force 1789) with the BILL OF RIGHTS (1791). The context: it was necessary TO REGULATE THE RELATIONS OF THE FORMER COLONIES AFTER THE BREAK WITH THE CROWN — to build a state ON A GREEN FIELD, without a monarch and without a historical constitution, so the order HAD TO BE WRITTEN DOWN.

cards.q: In what steps did constitutionalism spread across Europe?
cards.a: 1) 1791–1815 constitutions exported by French expansion. 2) 1812 THE CONSTITUTION OF CÁDIZ, a model for southern Europe and Latin America. 3) After the Congress of Vienna a wave of OCTROYED constitutions (the Charte 1814, Bavaria and Baden 1818) and MONARCHICAL CONSTITUTIONALISM arises. 4) THE BELGIAN CONSTITUTION OF 1831 as the most liberal model. 5) THE REVOLUTIONS OF 1848. 6) Stabilization (Austria 1867, Germany 1871). 7) After 1918 republican constitutions with constitutional jurisdiction.

slides.title: Source: the Pillersdorf Constitution (25 April 1848)
slides.text: THE SOURCE: '§ 8 The person of the Emperor is sacred and inviolable. He is not accountable for the exercise of governmental power; his instructions, however, must be countersigned by a responsible minister in order to take full effect. … § 45 All statutes require the assent of both chambers and the sanction of the Emperor.' WHAT CONSTITUTIONALISM IS: a political and legal movement according to which STATE POWER IS TO BE LIMITED AND DIVIDED BY A CONSTITUTION AND FUNDAMENTAL RIGHTS ARE TO BE GUARANTEED — government according to law, not according to caprice. FOR ITS BEGINNINGS see the previous section (America 1776/1787, France 1789/1791). THE RULER'S NON-ACCOUNTABILITY AND THE MINISTER'S RESPONSIBILITY: this is the heart of the matter and appears self-contradictory. The ruler is NOT ACCOUNTABLE because he is 'sacred and inviolable' — he cannot be sued, deposed or prosecuted; that is the inheritance of monarchical legitimacy. So that power should nevertheless not be uncontrolled, COUNTERSIGNATURE is introduced: the ruler's act takes effect only with a minister's counter-signature, AND BY IT THE MINISTER BECOMES RESPONSIBLE FOR IT. Together this yields the formula 'THE KING CAN DO NO WRONG' — because every step of his is a minister's step, for which the minister answers and can be called to account (impeachment of ministers, later also political responsibility to the chamber). The ruler therefore governs, but he cannot govern ALONE. THE EMPEROR'S ROLE IN LEGISLATION under § 45: a statute requires THE ASSENT OF BOTH CHAMBERS AND THE SANCTION OF THE EMPEROR, so the emperor has an ABSOLUTE VETO — without him no statute comes into being. He is therefore a full component of the legislative power, not merely the promulgator. ASSESSING THE AUSTRIAN DEVELOPMENT IN EUROPEAN COMPARISON: the Pillersdorf Constitution was OCTROYED (granted from above, not adopted by a constituent assembly), it was LATE (Belgium had a constitution as early as 1831) and it was SHORT-LIVED — after further upheavals it was succeeded by the Kremsier negotiations, then by the OCTROYED MARCH CONSTITUTION OF 1849 and finally by the SYLVESTER PATENTS OF 1851, which abolished constitutionalism for ten years (neo-absolutism). Only the OCTOBER DIPLOMA (1860), the FEBRUARY PATENT (1861) and the DECEMBER CONSTITUTION (1867) brought a lasting constitutional regime with fundamental rights and an Imperial Court. AUSTRIA THEREFORE BELONGS TO THE LATE, MONARCHICAL-CONSTITUTIONAL BRANCH — with a parliament but without parliamentary government, because the ministers were responsible to the emperor, not to the chamber; and with a long interruption such as western Europe did not know.

terms.def: A minister's counter-signature by which an act of the ruler takes effect and for which the minister is responsible.

cards.q: What is constitutionalism?
cards.a: A political and legal movement according to which STATE POWER IS TO BE LIMITED AND DIVIDED BY A CONSTITUTION AND FUNDAMENTAL RIGHTS ARE TO BE GUARANTEED — that is, government according to law, not according to caprice.

cards.q: How do the ruler's non-accountability and the minister's responsibility fit together?
cards.a: The ruler is NOT ACCOUNTABLE because he is 'sacred and inviolable' — he cannot be sued or deposed. So that power should not be uncontrolled, COUNTERSIGNATURE is introduced: his act takes effect only WITH A MINISTER'S COUNTER-SIGNATURE, AND BY IT THE MINISTER BECOMES RESPONSIBLE. Hence the formula 'THE KING CAN DO NO WRONG' — the ruler governs, but he cannot govern ALONE.

cards.q: How should the Austrian constitutional development be judged in European comparison?
cards.a: LATE AND MONARCHICAL-CONSTITUTIONAL. The Pillersdorf Constitution was OCTROYED, late (Belgium 1831) and short-lived — the March Constitution of 1849 followed, and then the SYLVESTER PATENTS OF 1851, which ABOLISHED constitutionalism for ten years. A lasting constitutional regime came only with the OCTOBER DIPLOMA (1860), the FEBRUARY PATENT (1861) and the DECEMBER CONSTITUTION (1867) — with a parliament but WITHOUT PARLIAMENTARY GOVERNMENT, because the ministers were responsible to the emperor, not to the chamber.

slides.title: Source: Rousseau and a sovereignty that cannot be represented
slides.text: THE SOURCE: 'Sovereignty cannot be represented, for the same reason that it cannot be alienated; it consists essentially in the general will, and will cannot be represented: either it is the same or it is other; there is no middle ground. The deputies of the people, therefore, are not and cannot be its representatives; they are merely its agents and can conclude nothing definitively. […] THE ENGLISH PEOPLE THINKS ITSELF FREE, BUT IT IS GREATLY MISTAKEN: IT IS FREE ONLY DURING THE ELECTION OF MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT. AS SOON AS THEY ARE ELECTED, SLAVERY OVERTAKES IT AND IT IS NOTHING.' (Du contrat social, 1762.) THE FRENCH JURIST WHO DEVELOPED THE CONCEPT OF SOVEREIGNTY TWO HUNDRED YEARS EARLIER IS JEAN BODIN (1530–1596) in LES SIX LIVRES DE LA RÉPUBLIQUE (1576), written out of the experience of the wars of religion. He defined sovereignty as a POWER SUPREME, PERPETUAL AND ABSOLUTE, whose principal mark is the RIGHT TO GIVE LAWS WITHOUT THE CONSENT OF OTHERS; the sovereign is bound only by divine and natural law and by the fundamental laws of the kingdom. ROMAN LAW AS THE BASIS OF THAT DOCTRINE: yes, and directly — Bodin draws on the concepts Roman law supplied about imperial power, especially Ulpian's 'PRINCEPS LEGIBUS SOLUTUS EST' (the prince is not bound by the laws) and 'QUOD PRINCIPI PLACUIT, LEGIS HABET VIGOREM' (what pleases the prince has the force of law), and on the construction of the LEX REGIA, by which the people was supposed to have transferred power to the emperor. Out of those building blocks one can construct absolutism and also — through the lex regia — the idea that power originally comes from the people. FOR ROUSSEAU THE BEARER OF SOVEREIGNTY IS ALWAYS THE PEOPLE, and inalienably so: it cannot transfer it, only exercise it itself. THE CONSTITUTIONAL REALITY OF HIS TIME: around 1762 ABSOLUTE MONARCHY prevails in Europe, usually in its enlightened form (France under Louis XV, Prussia under Frederick II, Austria under Maria Theresa, Russia under Catherine II). ENGLAND has a CONSTITUTIONAL MONARCHY with parliamentary government after 1689, and is thus the exception. DEMOCRACIES IN TODAY'S SENSE DID NOT EXIST IN EUROPE — the franchise was narrowly tied to property even in England; the nearest were small republics with assemblies of citizens, especially the SWISS CANTONS (Rousseau was himself a citizen of Geneva) and city republics such as Venice, which were however oligarchic. WHY HE CALLS THE ENGLISH SLAVES: because he criticizes THE REPRESENTATIVE PRINCIPLE AS SUCH — freedom, on his view, cannot be delegated, and whoever chooses a master once in a while is not free but merely picks his master. THE ELEMENT OF MODERN DEMOCRACY HE IS AIMING AT IS THEREFORE REPRESENTATIVE DEMOCRACY AND THE FREE MANDATE OF THE DEPUTY. Rousseau demands DIRECT democracy or at least an IMPERATIVE MANDATE, in which the deputy is a mere agent. And the irony of history: the revolution invoked Rousseau but introduced precisely the representation he rejected, and ART. 27 of the French constitution of 1791 expressly enshrined the FREE MANDATE.

terms.def: The prince is not bound by the laws — the Roman formula out of which Bodin builds absolute sovereignty.

slides.title: Source: Marbury v. Madison — the rule of law and judicial review
slides.text: SOURCE I: 'The very essence of civil liberty certainly consists in the right of every individual to claim the protection of the laws whenever he receives an injury. One of the first duties of government is to afford that protection. … The government of the United States has been emphatically termed A GOVERNMENT OF LAWS, AND NOT OF MEN. It will certainly cease to deserve that high appellation if the laws furnish no remedy for the violation of a vested legal right.' SOURCE II: 'The Constitution is either a superior, paramount law, unchangeable by ordinary means, or it is on a level with ordinary legislative acts, and, like other acts, is alterable when the legislature shall please to alter it. If the former part of the alternative be true, then a legislative act contrary to the Constitution IS NOT LAW; if the latter part be true, then written constitutions are absurd attempts on the part of the people to limit a power in its own nature illimitable.' (U.S. Supreme Court, Marbury v. Madison, 24 February 1803.) WHAT THE RULE OF LAW IS: government BOUND BY LAW, not by caprice — power is exercised only on the basis of and within the limits of the law, the laws are general, known in advance and the same for all (including the government), and their breach has a JUDICIALLY ENFORCEABLE REMEDY. The German variant RECHTSSTAAT stresses the legality of administration and judicial protection; the English RULE OF LAW (Dicey) stresses equality before the ordinary courts and the absence of a separate administrative law. WHAT SOURCE II ASSERTS ABOUT A WRITTEN CONSTITUTION: it poses an ALTERNATIVE WITH NO THIRD POSSIBILITY — either the constitution is PARAMOUNT LAW, and then a statute incompatible with it IS VOID, or it is an ordinary statute, and then a written constitution is absurd. Since the framers of written constitutions plainly meant them as fundamental and paramount law, it follows that A CONTRARY STATUTE IS NULL. THE CONSEQUENCES: for the LEGISLATOR, that he is bound by the constitution and cannot change it by an ordinary statute; for the JUDICIARY, that in a concrete dispute it must decide which of the two rules to apply — and thereby JUDICIAL REVIEW OF CONSTITUTIONALITY arises without the constitution expressly providing for it. COULD AN AMERICAN COURT DECIDE ON THE VALIDITY OF A STATUTE? YES, precisely from Marbury v. Madison, and in the form of DIFFUSE (decentralized) review: ANY COURT may review constitutionality in a concrete dispute (INCIDENTER) and the effect is the NON-APPLICATION of the statute in that case (INTER PARTES), not its annulment. WHY THIS WAS POSSIBLE SO EARLY PRECISELY IN THE USA: (1) the constitution was WRITTEN, adopted BY THE PEOPLE and designated THE SUPREME LAW OF THE LAND (the supremacy clause, Art. VI); (2) there was no monarch and no dogma of parliamentary sovereignty; (3) the FEDERAL STRUCTURE required someone to decide disputes of competence; (4) the common law tradition, in which a court routinely decides on the validity of norms of lower rank. AND THE SITUATION IN EUROPE AT THE TIME: judicial review did not exist. The principle of the SUPREMACY OF THE STATUTE prevailed, together with a distrust of judges inherited from the revolution (in France even a prohibition on judges interpreting statutes and the institution of the référé législatif); the Austrian IMPERIAL COURT (1867) could rule on violations of political rights but WAS NOT PERMITTED TO ANNUL STATUTES. ONLY THE AUSTRIAN CONSTITUTION OF 1920, on Kelsen's proposal, ESTABLISHED A CONSTITUTIONAL COURT WITH THE POWER TO ANNUL A STATUTE — a CONCENTRATED, ABSTRACT model with effect ERGA OMNES, the exact opposite of the American. That is the difference the exam asks about most often.

terms.def: American: any court, incidenter, effect inter partes. Austrian (Kelsen 1920): a single constitutional court, abstractly, effect erga omnes.

cards.q: What is the rule of law and how do the Rechtsstaat and the rule of law differ?
cards.a: Government BOUND BY LAW, not by caprice: power is exercised only on the basis of and within the limits of the law, the laws are general, known in advance and the same for all including the government, and a breach has a JUDICIALLY ENFORCEABLE REMEDY. The German RECHTSSTAAT stresses THE LEGALITY OF ADMINISTRATION AND JUDICIAL PROTECTION; the English RULE OF LAW (Dicey) stresses EQUALITY BEFORE THE ORDINARY COURTS and the absence of a separate administrative law.

cards.q: What alternative does Marbury v. Madison pose and what follows from it?
cards.a: AN ALTERNATIVE WITH NO THIRD POSSIBILITY: either the constitution is PARAMOUNT LAW, and then a contrary statute IS NOT LAW, or it is an ordinary statute, and then written constitutions are ABSURD ATTEMPTS. Since the framers meant them as paramount law, a contrary statute IS NULL — and the court must decide in a concrete dispute which rule to apply. Thereby JUDICIAL REVIEW arises without the constitution expressly providing for it.

cards.q: Why was judicial review possible so early in the USA?
cards.a: 1) The constitution was WRITTEN, adopted BY THE PEOPLE and designated THE SUPREME LAW OF THE LAND (the supremacy clause, Art. VI). 2) There was no monarch and no dogma of parliamentary sovereignty. 3) The FEDERAL STRUCTURE required someone to decide disputes of competence. 4) The COMMON LAW tradition, in which a court routinely decides on the validity of norms of lower rank.

cards.q: Compare the American and the Austrian model of constitutional review.
cards.a: THE AMERICAN (Marbury 1803) is DIFFUSE: ANY COURT may review, in a concrete dispute (INCIDENTER), and the effect is the NON-APPLICATION of the statute in that case (INTER PARTES). THE AUSTRIAN (the 1920 constitution, on Kelsen's proposal) is CONCENTRATED: A SINGLE CONSTITUTIONAL COURT, ABSTRACTLY, and it ANNULS the statute with effect ERGA OMNES. In Europe until then review did not exist — the SUPREMACY OF THE STATUTE prevailed and judges were distrusted; the Austrian Imperial Court (1867) was not permitted to annul statutes.

slides.title: The development of fundamental rights in Austria and how it differs
slides.text: THE DEVELOPMENT: (1) PRECURSORS UNDER ENLIGHTENED ABSOLUTISM — these are not rights but CONCESSIONS GRANTED FROM ABOVE: the Patent of Toleration (1781), the abolition of serfdom (1781), the abolition of torture (1776), the ABGB (1811) with its sentence about innate rights knowable by reason (§ 16), but without any guarantee against the state. (2) 1848 — the first catalogues: the Pillersdorf Constitution and above all the KREMSIER DRAFT, which was never adopted but was extraordinarily modern (it proceeded from the idea that all power comes from the people). (3) THE MARCH CONSTITUTION OF 1849 with its catalogue of rights — at once abolished by the SYLVESTER PATENTS OF 1851, which expressly revoked the fundamental rights. (4) 1867 — the BASIC LAW ON THE GENERAL RIGHTS OF CITIZENS (Staatsgrundgesetz, 21 December 1867): equality before the law, personal liberty, the inviolability of the home and of the secrecy of correspondence, freedom of expression and of the press, the rights of assembly and association, freedom of religion, of science and its teaching, free choice of occupation, protection of property, the equality of nationalities and languages (Art. 19). To this belongs the IMPERIAL COURT, before which protection of political rights could be sought. (5) The Basic Law on general rights outlived the monarchy and IS STILL IN FORCE IN AUSTRIA TODAY as part of the constitutional order, supplemented by the EUROPEAN CONVENTION (1958, with constitutional rank from 1964). HOW THE AUSTRIAN DEVELOPMENT DIFFERS FROM THE AMERICAN AND THE FRENCH: (a) IN ORIGIN — in the USA and France the rights are proclaimed REVOLUTIONARILY AND FROM BELOW as natural and pre-state; in Austria they are GRANTED BY THE RULER FROM ABOVE, that is, octroyed, so that what was given can also be taken away (as happened in 1851). (b) IN CHARACTER — the American and French rights are formulated as the INALIENABLE NATURAL RIGHTS OF MAN; the Austrian as the RIGHTS OF CITIZENS, that is, rights from the hand of the state, and subject in addition to the reservation of a statute. (c) IN GUARANTEE — in the USA enforceable in court against the legislator from 1803; in France long unenforceable (judicial review only with the Constitutional Council in 1958, full protection of rights only in 1971); in Austria the IMPERIAL COURT of 1867 protected rights against the ADMINISTRATION but not against a statute — review of statutes only from 1920. (d) IN THE DELAY AND INTERRUPTION, such as the western development did not know.

cards.q: How did fundamental rights develop in Austria?
cards.a: 1) Enlightened absolutism — not rights but CONCESSIONS FROM ABOVE (the Patent of Toleration 1781, the abolition of serfdom 1781 and of torture 1776, § 16 ABGB). 2) 1848 the first catalogues (Pillersdorf, the modern KREMSIER DRAFT). 3) The March Constitution of 1849 — abolished by the SYLVESTER PATENTS OF 1851. 4) 1867 the BASIC LAW ON THE GENERAL RIGHTS OF CITIZENS + the IMPERIAL COURT. 5) Still in force in Austria TODAY, supplemented by the ECHR (constitutional rank from 1964).

cards.q: How does the Austrian development of rights differ from the American and the French?
cards.a: IN ORIGIN: there REVOLUTIONARILY AND FROM BELOW as natural and pre-state, in Austria GRANTED FROM ABOVE — and what was given can be taken away (1851). IN CHARACTER: there the INALIENABLE RIGHTS OF MAN, in Austria the RIGHTS OF CITIZENS subject to the reservation of a statute. IN GUARANTEE: in the USA enforceable against the legislator from 1803; in Austria the Imperial Court (1867) protected only against the ADMINISTRATION, review of statutes only from 1920.
